turns.zh: 而且，实验不能成为公司里人做决策的方式。了解用户、理解市场、让你脑子把这些都连起来、知道客户想要什么样的体验——这些事多的是。如果科学数据，比如对成功概率的紧致判定，很重要，那绝对去做，因为那可能是你要做的一个重大战略转向，所以要个数据点来验证这堆额外工作值不值得。也可能是个超高频的页面，哪怕 0.1% 的差异都意味着几百万美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that was a big one to end on. That I think will help a lot of people avoid wasting time. Again, a whole other podcast conversation probably focus just on onboarding advice that you probably have, that I know you have. We've reached the last item. Is there anything else you want to share about this list before we move on?
turns.zh: 但除此之外，就该冲冲冲。做前后对比。顺便说，我不是说发了就走人。发了之后，做 24 小时、7 天、28 天的复盘，甚至一年后回来量一下和它相关的留存或延展数据。但什么都测，会废掉增长团队、把他们原地瘫痪。所以看看你的举措，问自己：哪里我需要精度？那里重要、我也能最好地拿到它；哪里就直接冲。我们在那儿也会失败，没关系，能撤回、能想办法改好。但失败反正都会发生。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: No, I think we've spent too much time. We're ready to go.
turns.zh: 统计上，p=0.05 很微妙。很多人把它当字面真理，其实它不过是个方向性数据点，说"大概有个新分布、均值可能不同，5% 的概率"。如果你测到 95% 统计显著，你可能根本没到那个程度，却把它当成铁律——"它能带来这么多提升"。所以我总觉得，在数据时代，人反而太不依赖自己的直觉了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not too much. Just enough time. And kind of on a note, I want to call an audible, and so we were going to talk through all of your favorite frameworks. I like the way this conversation has gone. I don't want people to get overwhelmed with information. So one idea is just list maybe your favorite growth frameworks just for folks to go check these out and not spend too much time on each one.
turns.zh: 很多反直觉的料。我太爱了。Elena，我们到第十条了。我知道第十条是特别的那种，是"不止一条"的连珠炮。快速开火。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yep, let's do that.
turns.zh: 所以第十条是我的小连珠炮环节。都是些我看着人花太多时间、却又心疼——因为它们根本不会带来任何结果。第一条：颜色优化。看在上帝份上，蓝就是蓝，蓝就是蓝。只要它可访问、够亮，就走吧。你不需要测蓝色的深浅、拿来和绿色比。选个颜色，继续，别在上面花时间。那是 2000 年代初的打法，早不灵了，科技行业早越过那阶段了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 第二条：第三方登录。很多时候我们想，哦，加了 Google 登录、Facebook 登录、Slack 登录、Microsoft 登录，随便哪种，就能多获客。有些情况下，第三方登录很重要。比如你是个开发者产品，请务必有 GitHub 登录——开发者本来就有那账号，让他们连上就行，别让他们新建。但如果你是个效率工具，邮箱就够用很久了。Gmail 挺好，但它不会给你带来更多获客。你只是做了个权宜之计，多两个人用而已。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Great. So the list of my favorite growth frameworks. And to me framework by the way, it's not a solution, it's a pattern. It's a pattern that exists across almost every single company out there and it's a starting point for your ideation and to figure out how you can almost shortcut to possible list of solutions as opposed to trying to figure out too hard of how to even define a problem on its own. So number one, it's probably expected if anybody has read anything or listened to me talk is growth loops. I think anybody who thinks about growth and anybody who thinks about growth in the funnel fashion versus understanding what the growth loops are is missing out on the ability to create sustainable growth engine. So it's very important to think about action, reaction that generates another action and it's a self-contained flywheel they can spin. A lot of resources on it at Reforge, Brian Balfour and Casey Winters and Andrew Chen wrote a lot about this. (01:16:33): Highly recommend anybody looking into. My next favorite growth framework's actually written by you, Lenny, and Dan, which is a race car framework. Everybody has a really hard time often thinking about what are all of them parts of growth initiatives and which are long-term, short-term, how much are they going to actually produce in results? And race car framework is wonderful because it separates different initiatives into, hey, there's some engines, loops that are just going to keep on spinning. There's some fuel that you're going to need to add into it, potentially like paid marketing dollars. There are some turbo boosts that you may have in your race car that are going to be, let's say big user conferences that you're going to hold as a product or there's [inaudible 01:17:22] and optimizations that you're going to need to do pouring oil into that engine so that actually performs correctly. It's beautiful. I talk about it all the time with everybody. (01:17:31): The next favorite growth framework for me comes from Bengali and that's adjacent to user theory. I think that was very powerful in terms of thinking about growth evolution. And as we talked about adding different growth models to your growth ecosystem, different growth loops, but also adjacent users which are outside of your ideal customer profiles or ICP, outside of your core user and how growth team can really bring them in and add additional oomph to your product without even expansion of product market fit by just optimizing their experiences. I'm going to stop at these three because I think those are the most powerful ones.
turns.zh: 它不会带来增量、不会提升激活、不会提升留存。它不是增长打法，只是你想投入的客户体验的一部分。连珠炮第三条：一次性邮件奇迹。我们太纠结"发给这一组客户的那一封邮件"了，心里嘀咕"天，它能带来多少提升"。它永远不会带来任何提升。单封邮件永远不可能见效。平均打开率太低，25%，最好的也就 40 到 50%。点的人更少。一封邮件永远做不成任何事。如果你要做邮件，请把它当成一系列沟通、当成它怎么和产品沟通互动的整体策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. On that last one, [inaudible 01:18:11] Bengali was on the podcast. We'll link to that episode if you want to go deeper on the adjacent using user theory. I love how that was a few minutes on things that could change people's life if they adopt one of these frameworks and learn how to think about growth in this way. It's such a powerful mental model for thinking about all this stuff you've been talking about this entire conversation.
turns.zh: 那是一整套策略，是一整个事。别纠结单封邮件。永远别去测单封邮件里的某个改动，永远不灵。你得把整套该死的东西做出来看效果，不是一封邮件，一封永远不成。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes, those frameworks are like my church in my mind of my system of beliefs of how I think about growth and how I think about it on a strategic level of owning it as a strategy, not just like a tactic or an initiative.
turns.zh: 这条我绝对有罪。这真的是条好建议，而且事后看太明显了，所以我很高兴你分享这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The church of Elena Verna. Amazing. Okay, so before we wrap up, I want to bring us over to Contrarian Corner, recurring segment on this podcast where I like to ask the guest if there's something they believe that most other people don't believe. Contrarian opinion you might say. Is there anything that comes to mind?
turns.zh: Elena Verna 的教堂。太妙了。好，收尾前，我想带到"逆向角落"——这播客的常驻环节，我喜欢问嘉宾有没有什么大多数人都不信、而你坚信的东西。算逆向观点吧。你脑中有什么吗？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I do have a very contrarian opinion, although it's not so much related to growth as opposed to maybe your personal growth and my contrarian opinion is that full-time jobs are not the best way to monetize the skill that you have. It's one of the packages that everybody should evaluate and take advantage of, but too many people blindly default to that package and don't explore other options that are both available on the market as well as best suited for their personalities, for their interests, and for their skill set. It's like a default plan that everybody subscribes to that is faulty in itself.
turns.zh: 我确实有个很逆向的观点，虽然它不那么关于增长，而更关于你个人的成长。我逆向的观点是：全职工作，不是把你技能变现的最好方式。它是每个人都该评估、利用的一揽子方案之一，但太多人盲目地默认选这个方案，不去探索市场上其他既可用、又最适合他们性格、兴趣和技能组合的选项。它就像人人都订阅的默认计划，而它本身是有缺陷的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. Wait, we got to hear more. So what are some other packages? I think we're buying some of these packages, these other options, but I guess what should people be thinking about when you say this in terms of what can they actually do and explore?
turns.zh: 哇。好。等等，我们得听更多。那还有哪些方案？我觉得我们正买着其中一些、这些别的选项，但当你说这个时，人们该从"自己实际能做什么、能探索什么"的角度去想？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I'll premise it to saying I don't want to rain parade on full-time roles. They're wonderful on video ability, to learn to get the expertise and depending on which career stage you are at full-time roles might be the absolute necessity for you to move on to and unlock the next level. However, full-time roles boxes into one company that may not be a great fit for us culturally, for our skills, for our ambitions, for our interests. Life is too short for that and ability to really go and figure out your own best monetization model, just like you work on that for your business, you should work for that on yourself without an assumption oftentimes is the only option that you should have. (01:20:56): So what are the other options? There's so many, obviously the couple known ones. Freelancing, you can be a contractor. I do a lot of advising and consulting because for my brain of how I work and how I like to puzzle solve and pattern match, it works much better to be horizontal across many companies versus vertical on one specific one. But that doesn't mean I still don't take those vertical engagements to deepen my knowledge into any specific topic. But overall it's a lot more interesting for me to pattern match across multiple companies and help them grow as opposed to just focusing on one. (01:21:34): There's interim engagements where there's a predetermined end date to your agreement. There's fractional engagements where you're working part-time on something as opposed to engulfing yourself completely. There's other ways to create courses, there's a way to create newsletters and monetize them like you're doing such a fantastic job. So there's just so many options and people are sometimes paralyzed by fear of instability, that it creates when you start to explore other options because you don't have that contract with that one company that provides you that paycheck every two weeks to rely on. But at the same time you can create diversification for your career and you depend on when you need to pull that trigger and when is the right time for you to explore. But to spend your entire career only assuming full-time is the only way I think is a complete mistake that a lot of people are doing.
turns.zh: 我先铺垫一句：我不想给全职角色泼冷水。它们在让你学到专长、拿到专业能力上很棒，而且取决于你处在哪个职业阶段，全职角色可能是你进阶、解锁下一关的绝对必需。但全职角色把你框进一家公司——而那家公司可能在文化、技能、野心、兴趣上都不那么适合你。人生苦短，而且你真该去搞清楚自己最好的变现模型，就像你为业务那样去经营自己，不要假设全职往往是你唯一该有的选项。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of my favorite posts of yours along these lines, which is around increasing... What you want to do is increase optionality and I guess talk about that because I think it's a really powerful piece of advice.
turns.zh: 那还有哪些选项？多了去了，几个知名的：自由职业，你可以当承包商。我做很多顾问和咨询，因为就我脑子的工作方式、我喜欢解谜和模式匹配而言，横向跨很多公司、比纵向扎进一家具体公司要适合得多。但这不代表我不接那些纵向项目去深挖某个具体话题。但整体上，跨多家公司做模式匹配、帮它们增长，比只盯一家有趣多了。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: So this advice of career optionality, being the ultimate north star for anybody in their professional journey is something that I'm very strong on because a lot of people have the goal of, I don't know, maybe I want to be a VP or I want to become a CEO. Or I don't know, I want to be a manager and I want to people manage. And this becomes their north star and they start working towards it. But a lot of people when they get to their perceived corporate ladder north stars find themselves extremely dissatisfied, depressed even by how terrible that job is. Could people manage your job? I wouldn't wish it on my worst enemy because it's a terrible job if you don't enjoy it and you don't know if you're going to like it until you actually do it. (01:23:33): So I think setting a title as your goal, which so many of us have titles as goals, is very wrong way to think about it as opposed to saying, "Hey, my goal professional is actually to have options so I can choose what I want to do. So I can choose what fits my life right now that I can choose what fits my skills and that fits my personality and that makes me happy." (01:23:54): And to get career optionality, if that's your goal, you start thinking about your progression a lot differently. You're not starting to think about it of what will get me to the next title. You start thinking about what will can I do next year that will increase my option pool? And that's very different than just getting to a higher title. And if you start thinking about evaluating opportunities or whether you should stay at the company, whether you should move at the company from the lens of does it increase my options if I stay at this company for one more year or does it keep it the same or does it actually potentially decrease? That is the right way to find your ultimate happy place and happy job that brings you energy, that brings you happiness versus just going for a title and then being very disappointed with what that brings along with it.
turns.zh: 还有临时聘约，协议里有预定好的结束日期。还有兼职聘约，你只做部分时间，而不是把自己完全吞进去。还有别的方式做课程、做简报并变现——就像你做得那么出色。所以选项实在太多，而人有时被"不稳定带来的恐惧"给瘫痪了，因为你开始探索别的选项时，没有那份每两周发一次薪水的公司合同可依赖。但与此同时，你能给自己的职业造出多元化，你来决定什么时候该扣扳机、什么时候是探索的好时机。但把整个职业生涯都只假定全职是唯一出路，我觉得是太多人都在犯的一个彻头彻尾的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing advice. So important and something I'll add that I think is a balance to what people may be feeling here is like, oh, I'll just bounce around all the best logo companies and create this killer resume. I think you also need to build depth and actual experience that you can tap into if you do any of these things. For example, a lot of people want to jump to like I'm going to be a newsletter person, I'm going to start a podcast, be an advisor before they've done anything real and you have nothing to actually base your advice on and that part is very important.
turns.zh: 你这方面我最爱的帖子之一，是关于提升……你想做的是提升"选择权"。我想让你聊聊这个，因为我觉得这是条极有力的建议。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: You have to earn your right to unlock optionality and earning that right does usually lie within full-time jobs. That is a universal truth. But then at some point you should start not just looking at full- time jobs as the only option that you have. You should start to think about when can you start unlocking new ones and testing the market on it.
turns.zh: 这条"职业选择权"作为任何人职业旅程的终极北极星，我是极其笃定的——因为很多人目标是"我想当 VP"或"我想当 CEO"，或"我想当经理、管理人"。这成了他们的北极星，他们朝它努力。但很多到了他们想象的职场阶梯北极星的人，发现自己对那份工作极其不满、甚至抑郁——因为那工作可能糟透了。"管理人"这活儿你干得了吗？我可不希望我死对头干这个，因为如果你不享受它、又不知道自己会不会喜欢，直到你真干了才知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other point is that you've been a great example of is it's not a one-way door. You can have full-time job, go to something else, go back to full-time job, be an advisor, be an intern person, be a newsletter person. You do that really well.
turns.zh: 所以把头衔当目标——我们太多人把头衔当目标——是错的思路。该说的是："嘿，我职业上的目标，其实是拥有选择权，好让我能选我想做的、选适合我当下生活的、选适合我技能、适合我性格、让我开心的。"而要获得职业选择权，如果那是你的目标，你思考进阶的方式会大不一样。你不会再去想"什么能让我升到下个头衔"，而会想"明年我能做什么来扩大我的选项池？"这和单纯升头衔非常不同。如果你从"留在这公司再一年，是增加我的选项、保持不变、还是其实在减少？"这个透镜去评估机会、决定该不该留、该不该走——那才是找到终极幸福归宿、幸福工作的正道，它给你能量、给你快乐，而不是只冲头衔、然后被随之而来的东西大失所望。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: You should have to do it all. It's all a menu of options and you pick a menu item that fits your best in any given point of your life. It's never say never and never shut the door on anything. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 太赞的建议。太重要了。我要补一点平衡——我猜有人听了会觉得"哦，那我就随便跳去各大招牌公司、攒一份杀手级简历"。我觉得你也需要建起深度和真实经验，无论做哪样你都能调用。比如很多人想直接跳去"我要做简报人、我要开播客、当顾问"，却还没干过任何真实的事，你根本没有东西撑起你的建议，而那部分极其重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god, Elena, this was incredible. Before we get to our very exciting lighting round, is there anything else you want to share or leave listeners with, maybe a last nugget or thought or not because covered a lot already.
turns.zh: 你得挣来解锁选择权的资格，而挣这资格通常就落在全职工作里。这是个普世真理。但在某个时点，你该开始不把全职当成你唯一拥有的选项。你该开始想：我什么时候能开始解锁新选项、在市场上试试水。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: No, I think we've covered so much. I don't want to overwhelm.
turns.zh: 另一点你是个好榜样——它不是一扇单向门。你可以有全职、跳去别的、再回全职、当顾问、当时段人士、当简报人。你这点做得真漂亮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 你该全都经历一遍。这是一整份选项菜单，你在人生任何阶段，挑最合你当下的一款。永远别说永不，也永远别对任何事关门。绝对。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes, I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我的天，Elena，这太了不起了。在我们进入超精彩的闪电回合前，你还有什么想分享、或留给听众的——也许最后一颗干货或想法，或者不用，因为已经聊太多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, surprise, surprise. What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 不，我觉得我们覆盖得够多了。不想让人信息过载。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Okay, so I just finished this book that I love so much, it's not a professional book, but it's Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir. It's the same author that wrote Martian. Martian also was made into a movie. So good, so good. Can't put it down. I think I read it like two days straight. So highly recommend that. And the next one that I also started reading right now is Body Burst. Body Burst is so good. It's actually takes into account AI and how we can upload our consciousness in AI and what can happen with that. So highly recommend that, I think it's actually closer to what potentially can be in the truth for us in the future than not. But I'm a big sci-fi geek, so I read mostly sci-fi books.
turns.zh: 来吧。那么，我们到了超精彩的闪电回合。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a sci-fi recommendation for you that comes from Noah Smith. I love his newsletters called Noah Opinion and he has a list of his favorite sci-fi books that I've been working my way through. It's called, you may have read it by Werner Vogel, Fire Upon The Deep. Have you heard of this?
turns.zh: 准备好了。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: No, I have not.
turns.zh: 第一个问题，毫不意外：你最常推荐给别人的一两本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. It's described as not a sci-fi but space, like a space opera where it's epic, the most epic scale of universe story.
turns.zh: 好，我刚读完一本超爱的书，不是专业书，是 Andy Weir 的《Project Hail Mary》（拯救号行动）。就是写《火星救援》那位，那本也被拍成了电影。太好看了，根本放不下，我大概连着两天读完。强力推荐。下一本是我在读的《Body Burst》（身体爆发），也超棒。它其实把 AI、以及我们怎么把意识上传到 AI、会发生什么都考虑进去了。所以我很推荐，我觉得它其实比不接近，而是更接近我们未来可能的真相。但我是个科幻迷，基本只读科幻。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I'll download it tonight, it'll be on my list.
turns.zh: 我给你个科幻推荐，来自 Noah Smith。我超爱他的简报《Noah Opinion》，他有个最爱科幻书单，我正一本本啃。叫《Fire Upon The Deep》（深渊之火），作者 Werner Vogel，你也许读过？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It takes a little bit to get into. It's quite unique, but you just keep going and it's incredible and AI plays a big role in it actually.
turns.zh: 没，我没读过。

Because we can all laugh at the absurdity of the lives that we live in every single day. And a picture's worth a thousand words. And sometimes memes are just the best way to communicate the most complex situations that we are facing within our corporate world. And they help us understand how common all of those situations are. We're not unique. You're not feeling alone by feeling down about what happened. Everybody's going through the same thing. So that's why I love memes because they help connect people on both sides. (01:32:05): Even if you're making fun of one side because they're like, yeah, that is true and this is so funny. (01:32:26): But my favorite meme is actually one of the first ones that I've created and I think it's from Family Guy where they have an elephant and the penguin standing and then there's Moses I think, or some biblical character saying, "What the hell is this?"
